title: The Pharmacist's Son: Schwabing, the Six Days of the Räterepublik, and Oranienburg
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Berlin, born to the apothecary
stops.date_confidence: attested. Exact birth address not established in any source consulted; the coordinate marks central Berlin. The parents' names are given correctly here after correction: father Siegfried Seligmann Mühsam, mother Rosalie née Cohn. Some secondary accounts garble the mother's surname to Seligmann.
stops.campa: On the sixth of April 1878 a third child is born in Berlin to Siegfried Mühsam, pharmacist, and his wife Rosalie, born Cohn. The family is Jewish, prosperous, orderly. The father will sit on the Lübeck city council from 1887 to 1915 and expects his sons to enter trades a council can respect. The boy is named Erich. Within the year the Mühsams leave the capital for the north, and the city that will hold his best journals and his last arrest becomes, for the time being, only the entry on a certificate. He does not live in Berlin again for twenty-two years.
suggested_refs: The Lübeck council records naming Siegfried Mühsam as a city councillor, 1887-1915
sources: German Resistance Memorial Center (GDW Berlin), Mühsam biography

stops.name: Lübeck, the house on the Mengstraße
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the move and the address (Stolpersteine Lübeck biographical file, Mengstraße 4); the year is a reconstruction. Sources give the move variously as 'soon after birth', 'at six weeks', and 'at one year'; the contradiction is not resolved here and the day and month are set only to order the segment.
stops.campa: The family settles at Mengstraße 4 in Lübeck, a merchant street in the old town, and Siegfried opens his pharmacy. Erich grows up here with three siblings under a Hanseatic respectability that measures a life by its counter and its ledger. When exactly the move happens the record will not say: soon after the birth, at six weeks, at a year, depending on which account is opened. The city of his childhood is not the city of his birth, and no source consulted settles the month in which that became true.
suggested_refs: The Stolpersteine Lübeck biographical dossier for Mengstraße 4

stops.name: Lübeck, expelled from the Katharineum
stops.date_confidence: attested. The expulsion is dated 11 January 1896 in the German record, for 'sozialdemokratische Umtriebe'. Note a correction against widely circulated English accounts: he is seventeen at the time, not sixteen, having been born 6 April 1878. The years of attendance from 1888 are inferred from his age, not documented in sources consulted.
stops.campa: He passes school matters to the Lübecker Volksbote, the Social Democratic paper, including a piece mocking a teacher, and on the eleventh of January 1896 the Katharineum expels him for social-democratic agitation. The humanist Gymnasium of a Hanseatic city has rules about corporal punishment and about boys who write to socialists, and he has broken the second while resenting the first. His father, a city councillor, learns of it publicly, and the household of an elected man now contains a boy the school has entered in its books as an agitator. He is seventeen years old.
stops.quote: Even at a young age, I realized that the state apparatus determined the injustice of all social institutions. To fight the state and the forms in which it expresses itself–capitalism, imperialism, militarism, class domination, political judiciary, and oppression of any kind–has always been the motivation for my actions.
stops.quote_source: Erich Mühsam, Autobiography (written 1919), in Liberating Society from the State and Other Writings: A Political Reader, ed. and trans. Gabriel Kuhn (PM Press, 2011), printed p. 26. Kuhn's headnote establishes the text as the 1919 original, not the 1927 additions; it is written in Bavarian custody about the Lübeck childhood.
suggested_refs: The Lübecker Volksbote for January 1896
Kuhn's editorial headnote on the dating of the Selbstbiographie, printed p. 25

stops.name: Parchim, the rural Gymnasium
stops.date_confidence: attested that he finished schooling at the Friedrich-Franz-Gymnasium in Parchim, Mecklenburg, after the Lübeck expulsion; month and day are set only to order the segment.
stops.campa: Expelled from Lübeck, he is sent inland to Mecklenburg to finish at the Friedrich-Franz-Gymnasium in Parchim, a small-town school with no newspaper scandal attached to it. The arrangement is his father's: keep the boy in education, keep him away from the Volksbote, get him a leaving certificate. Parchim is a market town on flat country, sixty miles from the Baltic and from everyone who knows what he did. He is boarded out among strangers, sits his final examinations, and comes home in possession of the certificate his father wanted.
suggested_refs: Records of the Friedrich-Franz-Gymnasium, Parchim

stops.name: Lübeck, apprenticed at the Adler-Apotheke
stops.date_confidence: attested that the apprenticeship was served in Lübeck at the Adler-Apotheke, correcting an earlier identification as the Ratsapotheke; the coordinate still carries the older figure and should be moved once the Adler-Apotheke address is confirmed. Month and day set to order the segment. A second apprenticeship stage at Blomberg in Lippe (51.9331, 9.0831) appears in the erichinenglish chronology alone and is corroborated by neither German Wikipedia nor the chronology's own later summary; it is carried here as [R] inside the campa rather than given a stop of its own.
stops.campa: At his father's insistence he begins a pharmacist's apprenticeship in Lübeck, at the Adler-Apotheke, weighing out powders in the trade his father chose for him. One chronology adds a further stage in the small Lippe town of Blomberg; no other source knows of it. He serves his time. He has no taste for the counter and no way past it yet, and every account of these years, including his own, treats them as a sentence rather than a training. None of them records him taking the slightest interest in the work.
suggested_refs: The Adler-Apotheke, Lübeck
theanarchistlibrary.org, erichinenglish.org chronology, for the disputed Blomberg stage

stops.name: Berlin, the pharmacy on the Weddingplatz
stops.date_confidence: attested to autumn 1900, with the post quit before the year is out. The square is the Weddingplatz in Berlin-Wedding; the form 'Wedingplatz' reproduces a typographical error in the erichinenglish chronology, and the coordinate has been corrected accordingly.
stops.campa: He comes back to the city of his birth at twenty-two and takes a post at a pharmacy on the Weddingplatz, in the working district north of the centre. He holds it a few weeks. Before the year is out he quits, and with it the trade entirely: no counter, no certificate, no father's plan. He has no income and no profession and is about to acquire neither. From this winter on he never holds a salaried post again. Everything he lives on for the next thirty-four years comes from writing, from lecturing, or from other people.
suggested_refs: The Weddingplatz, Berlin-Wedding, site of his last employment in pharmacy

stops.name: Berlin, rooms on the Augsburger Straße
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the address and the turn to freelance writing; month and day set to order the segment.
stops.campa: He takes rooms on the Augsburger Straße behind the Kurfürstendamm and calls himself a writer, which at this point means unpaid. The west of Berlin in 1901 is full of such rooms and such men: cabaret verse, small magazines, coffee bought on credit, an argument running for three days across four addresses. He begins to publish: verse and cabaret texts, from 1901 onward, none of it paying the rent. In December 1900 he meets Heinrich Hart, and through the Hart brothers, within the year, Gustav Landauer.
suggested_refs: Mühsam's earliest published verse and cabaret texts, Berlin 1901-1903

stops.name: Schlachtensee, the Neue Gemeinschaft
stops.date_confidence: attested that he is deeply involved with the Hart brothers' Neue Gemeinschaft from 1901 and that the friendship with Gustav Landauer begins in the same year; month and day set to order the segment. Correcting a conflation in the source material: the Neue Gemeinschaft colony was founded in 1902 at Schlachtensee, Seestraße 33-37, on Berlin's western edge, not in Friedrichshagen on the east, which was only its predecessor milieu. Mühsam did move to Friedrichshagen in 1902, as a residence.
stops.campa: The Hart brothers gather a utopian-literary community on the western edge of Berlin and call it the Neue Gemeinschaft: shared house, shared table, lectures on the coming order of things. Mühsam attaches himself to it, and there he sits at a table with Gustav Landauer, nine years older, already a translator and a convict, already convinced that socialism is built and not seized. Landauer will be his teacher for eighteen years. The colony house stands at Seestraße 33-37 in Schlachtensee, founded in 1902, and it does not last long.
suggested_refs: The Neue Gemeinschaft colony house, Seestraße 33-37, Schlachtensee (today Am Schlachtensee 50-58)

segments.name: The Mountain and the Wander Years

stops.name: Monte Verità, the hill above Ascona
stops.date_confidence: attested that he lived at the Ascona colony in 1904 and published the small book Ascona (Locarno, 1905) about the colonists; month and day set to order the segment. Correcting the source pool: the friendship that begins here is with Karl Gräser, not with Landauer, whom he had already met in Berlin in 1901. The coordinate is inherited byte-identical from karl_graser.journey.json.
stops.campa: He climbs the Ticino hillside to the colony of vegetarians, nudists, theosophists and anarchists that Henri Oedenkoven, Ida Hofmann and the brothers Karl and Gusto Gräser have made on Monte Verità, and he stays. Out of the visit comes a short book, Ascona, printed at Locarno in 1905, the first sustained account anyone writes of the colony from inside it. On Karl Gräser the book is favourable, and favourable about the practice rather than the doctrine. He goes up to Gräser's plot and watches a man live exactly what he says.
stops.quote: Gräser ist der erste Mensch, der mir begegnet ist, der mit starrer Konsequenz das, was er theoretisch als richtig erkannt hat, in die Praxis umsetzt.
stops.quote_source: Erich Mühsam, Ascona (Locarno, 1905), on Karl Gräser, as carried in karl_graser.journey.json
suggested_refs: Erich Mühsam, Ascona (Locarno: Verlag Carlo Frizzi, 1905)

stops.name: Ascona, the death of Lotte Hattemer
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the death and the date. Mühsam's own whereabouts on 19 April 1906 are not established in the sources consulted, and the stop is placed here because he is named in the rumour that follows, not because his presence is documented. The manner of death is contested and the contradiction is left open: an official's daughter's suicide by the 1909 police report, a poisoning administered by a physician by another account.
stops.campa: Lotte Hattemer, one of the seven founding colonists of Monte Verità, dies at Ascona at twenty-nine. The police file of 1909 will call it suicide; another account has a physician administering poison. The colony's own rumour names Johannes Nohl, and it names Mühsam, who had published his book about the place the year before. Where he was on the nineteenth of April 1906 is not established in any source consulted. What he did or did not know is nowhere on record, then or afterwards.
suggested_refs: The 1909 Ascona police report on the death of Lotte Hattemer

stops.name: Paris, the last of the wander years
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Paris, Zürich and Vienna are all named among the wander-years destinations of roughly 1904 to 1908 in the German record; no addresses, durations or specific stays are attested for any of them, and no Mühsam address in Paris was located in this pass. The coordinate is the canonical Paris pin inherited byte-identical from the interlock lens; the Zürich and Vienna figures in the geography lens (47.3769, 8.5417 and 48.2103, 16.3659) are illustrative of the milieu only. Month and day are set only to order the segment.
stops.campa: Between Switzerland and Bavaria there are four or five years with no fixed address in them. Zürich, Vienna, Paris: each has its anarchist press, its cheap rooms, its coffeehouse standing in for an office. The record of the period is thin, a city name and a season at a time. In these same years he writes the pamphlet Die Jagd auf Harden on the Eulenburg affair, defending a man hunted for his sexuality by a press that has worked out how well the hunt sells. He will take up the case of whoever is being destroyed lawfully for the rest of his life, and this is the first clear instance of it.
suggested_refs: Erich Mühsam, Die Jagd auf Harden (1908)
sources: theanarchistlibrary.org, Souchy chronology of Erich Mühsam

stops.name: Berlin, the Sozialistischer Bund
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the founding, with a discrepancy left open: the GDW Berlin biography gives May 1908, gustav_landauer.journey.json gives June 1908 with twelve articles. The coordinate is the canonical Berlin pin inherited byte-identical from gustav_landauer.journey.json. The exact venue is not specified in any source consulted. Martin Buber's co-membership is carried from the Landauer file and tagged [R] there.
stops.campa: Landauer draws up twelve articles and founds the Sozialistischer Bund, a federation of small settlement-groups meant to build socialism outside the party and outside the state rather than by capturing either. Mühsam joins, alongside Martin Buber. It is the organisational form he argues for until the end, and what he likes in it is that nobody in it is waiting for permission. From 1909 he runs two of the Bund's Munich subgroups himself, and names them Tat and Anarchist.
suggested_refs: Gustav Landauer's twelve articles of the Sozialistischer Bund, Berlin 1908
sources: German Resistance Memorial Center (GDW Berlin), Mühsam biography

segments.name: Schwabing and the Journal Called Cain

stops.name: Munich-Schwabing, the quarter that keeps him
stops.date_confidence: attested that he settles in Munich-Schwabing in 1909; month and day set to order the segment. Correcting the source pool, which had this move and the verse collection Der Krater three years early at 1906: both belong to 1909. He is documented as a Stammgast of the Café Stefanie, which stood at Amalienstraße and Theresienstraße in Maxvorstadt (48.1478, 11.5767), not in Schwabing, and the attestation covers the Munich years from 1909, not earlier.
stops.campa: At thirty-one he stops moving and settles in Schwabing, and the second verse collection, Der Krater, appears the same year. The quarter runs on cheap rooms, models, painters, Russian students and police informers, and its parliament sits at the Café Stefanie over on the Amalienstraße. For the next ten years Munich knows exactly where to find him, and he is enough of a fixture there that Johannes R. Becher puts him into a poem about the place in 1912. He is a small bald man with a red beard, thick glasses and a good singing voice.
suggested_refs: Erich Mühsam, Der Krater (1909)
Johannes R. Becher's 1912 poem on the Café Stefanie

stops.name: Munich, the unemployed on the Marienplatz
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The demonstration is reported in Souchy's chronology of Mühsam and is not corroborated in the German record consulted; month and day are set only to order the segment. The coordinate is the Marienplatz, Munich's central square.
stops.campa: The Tat group brings the unemployed of Munich onto the Marienplatz, under the town hall and the Marian column. It is not a large demonstration. It obtains nothing, and no newspaper of record keeps an account of it. He has spent nine years among people who discuss the coming order over coffee. The Bavarian police do not care what is discussed over coffee; they care about a man who puts the unemployed into a square. They open a file on him in 1909 and keep adding to it until 1919. Souchy's chronology is the only source consulted that reports the day at all.
suggested_refs: Bavarian police files on the Tat group, 1909-1914
sources: theanarchistlibrary.org, Souchy chronology of Erich Mühsam

stops.name: Munich, the founding of Kain
stops.date_confidence: attested to April 1911. The end date is corrected against the source pool: Kain ran from 1911 to 1919, suspended for the duration of the First World War and resumed in 1918-19, not stopped for good in August 1914. The editorial address is not confirmed; the coordinate marks central Schwabing.
stops.campa: From his own rooms he launches Kain: Zeitschrift für Menschlichkeit, a monthly he writes almost entirely himself. The name is the first murderer's and the subtitle is journal for humanity, and he means the pairing exactly: humanity is to be looked for wherever the order has put its mark. He prints anarcho-communist argument, verse, obituaries, court reports, and quarrels, most of it against the two things he holds to be one thing, capital and the nation. It runs until the war shuts it, and resumes when the war ends.
suggested_refs: Kain: Zeitschrift für Menschlichkeit, Munich, 1911-1914 and 1918-1919
sources: German Resistance Memorial Center (GDW Berlin), Mühsam biography

stops.name: Munich, marriage to Zenzl Elfinger
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1915 in Souchy's chronology; English Wikipedia gives only the year. The registry office is not named in any source consulted and the coordinate marks the Munich city centre. Day set to order the segment.
stops.campa: He marries Kreszentia Elfinger, called Zenzl, the widow of a Bavarian farmer and no part of the Schwabing world at all. She is practical where he is voluble, and she stays. He keeps other affairs and does not hide them. She remains his companion for the nineteen years he has left, and for twenty-eight years after that she carries his papers across two dictatorships and is punished by both. Which registry office they marry in is not named in any source consulted.
suggested_refs: Zenzl Mühsam's later testimony, gathered in Rudolf Rocker, Der Leidensweg von Zensl Mühsam (Berlin: Verlag Die Freie Gesellschaft, 1949)
sources: theanarchistlibrary.org, Souchy chronology of Erich Mühsam

stops.name: Munich, the Kakaostube on the Karlsplatz
stops.date_confidence: attested by Mühsam's own diary for 15 July 1916, which does not name the friend Guttzeit wants him to meet; the reconstruction rests on that single source. Coordinate inherited from johannes_friedrich_guttzeit.journey.json.
stops.campa: On the fifteenth of July Johannes Friedrich Guttzeit telephones the flat and asks him to come to the Kakaostube on the Karlsplatz: there is a friend visiting from neutral Switzerland who would like to meet him. Mühsam goes. It is the third year of the war and a man arriving from outside the blockade carries news that no German paper is permitted to print. The diary records the telephone call, the walk across town, and the meeting. It does not record the friend's name.
suggested_refs: Mühsam's diary for 15 July 1916, muehsam-tagebuch.de

stops.name: Traunstein, six months in the fortress
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the sentence, corrected as to its nature: this is Festungshaft, fortress confinement of six months, imposed for breaching his ban on political activity and for refusing to serve in the Vaterländischer Hilfsdienst. It is not a banishment from Munich, as several English accounts have it, and those accounts and the separate 'arrest as an antiwar agitator, April 1918' describe the same event twice. The precise date 24 April 1918 is unattested in the German record; month set to order the segment.
stops.campa: Having argued himself, under pressure from other anarchists, out of any early sympathy for the German war and into open agitation against it, he is arrested for breaking his ban on political activity and for refusing the patriotic labour service, and sentenced to six months in the fortress at Traunstein. Traunstein is a small town at the foot of the Chiemgau Alps. He is still inside it in the autumn, when the fleet mutinies at Kiel and the whole apparatus that put him there begins to come apart.
suggested_refs: The fortress at Traunstein, Upper Bavaria
sources: German Resistance Memorial Center (GDW Berlin), Mühsam biography

stops.name: Munich, back for the revolution
stops.date_confidence: attested. English Wikipedia dates his release to 3 November 1918 and the Munich revolution to the night of 7-8 November; the German record has him taking part in the overthrow of the Wittelsbach monarchy alongside Kurt Eisner's Independent Social Democrats.
stops.campa: On the seventh of November Kurt Eisner and the Independent Social Democrats put an end to seven hundred years of Wittelsbach rule in Bavaria without a shot fired in Munich, and Mühsam is out of the fortress and in the streets for it. A journalist, a theatre critic and a poet have taken a kingdom. For a few weeks it looks to him as though the argument he has been making since the Neue Gemeinschaft has simply come true. Kain resumes publication after four silent years.
suggested_refs: Kain, resumed series, Munich 1918-1919
sources: German Resistance Memorial Center (GDW Berlin), Mühsam biography
theanarchistlibrary.org, Souchy chronology of Erich Mühsam

stops.name: Munich, arrested by the revolution's own order
stops.date_confidence: attested in Souchy's chronology; the exact place of arrest is not specified and the coordinate marks the Munich city centre.
stops.campa: On the tenth of January the Minister-President of revolutionary Bavaria orders the arrest of members of the Revolutionäre Arbeiterrat, and Mühsam is among them. A revolution acquires a state faster than it acquires anything else, and the state then behaves like one. Nine weeks after the monarchy falls, the government the revolution made is jailing the council-communists who think it stopped too early, and one of them is the man who was in the street for it in November. He is held briefly. Souchy's chronology does not say where in Munich they take him.
suggested_refs: Records of the Revolutionäre Arbeiterrat, Munich, winter 1918-1919
sources: theanarchistlibrary.org, Souchy chronology of Erich Mühsam

stops.name: Munich, the motion at the Rätekongress
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the motion and its rejection, corrected as to date: the German record attaches the rejection of Mühsam's motion to proclaim a Räterepublik to the Bavarian Rätekongress of 25 February 1919, not 28 February. A vote tally of 234 to 70 circulates in secondary summaries and could not be traced to any reachable source; it is omitted here rather than repeated. The venue within Munich is not specified. Kurt Eisner was shot on 21 February 1919, four days before, by Anton Graf von Arco auf Valley.
stops.campa: Four days after Kurt Eisner is shot dead in the Promenadestraße on his way to deliver his own resignation speech, the Congress of Soldiers', Workers' and Peasants' Councils meets in a city with no government. Mühsam moves that the Räterepublik be proclaimed. The congress votes him down. The state Eisner made has lost its head and has not yet lost its reflexes, and the men in the hall are not ready to do without one. The Räterepublik they vote down on the twenty-fifth of February is proclaimed on the seventh of April.
suggested_refs: Proceedings of the Bayerischer Rätekongress, Munich, February 1919

stops.name: Munich, the Wittelsbacher Palais
stops.date_confidence: attested. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from gustav_landauer.journey.json, where it was corrected to the palace at Brienner Straße 20. The geography lens gave 48.1429, 11.5776 for the same building; the Landauer figure is preferred as the corrected one.
stops.campa: The Bavarian Council Republic is proclaimed on the seventh of April at the Wittelsbacher Palais on the Brienner Straße, and the men who proclaim it are a playwright, a philosopher of stateless socialism and a cabaret poet. Ernst Toller leads it. Gustav Landauer takes the commission for public enlightenment, education and the arts. Mühsam sits in the same government. Their enemies will call it the regime of the coffeehouse anarchists, and about the composition of the cabinet the insult is not wrong. It lasts six days.
suggested_refs: The Wittelsbacher Palais, Brienner Straße 20, Munich, demolished after 1944
sources: theanarchistlibrary.org, Souchy chronology of Erich Mühsam

stops.name: Munich, taken on Palm Sunday
stops.date_confidence: attested. Correcting a causal error in the source pool: the arrest happens on 13 April 1919 during the Palmsonntagsputsch, that is BEFORE the communist-led second council republic, which is why he takes no part in it. The Freikorps and Reichswehr suppression follows only on 2-3 May 1919. The exact site of arrest is not specified.
stops.campa: On Palm Sunday the republican guard moves against the council government and Mühsam is arrested in Munich and taken out of the city to the penitentiary at Ebrach. Everything that follows in Munich happens without him: the second council republic under Leviné and the communists, the hostages shot in the Luitpold-Gymnasium, and in the first days of May thirty thousand Freikorps and Reichswehr troops retaking the city street by street. He is behind the walls at Ebrach, a hundred and fifty miles to the north, before any of the shooting begins.
suggested_refs: The Palmsonntagsputsch, Munich, 13 April 1919
sources: German Resistance Memorial Center (GDW Berlin), Mühsam biography

segments.name: Five and a Half Years of Fortress

stops.name: Ebrach, the news about Landauer
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the diary entry, headed 'Gustav Landauer's Death' and dated May 1919 at Ebrach in the Kuhn edition; day set to order the segment. Landauer was taken to Stadelheim on 2 May 1919 and beaten and shot there by Freikorps troops. Mühsam is at Ebrach and not present, which is the point of the entry.
stops.campa: Word reaches Ebrach that Gustav Landauer has been taken to Stadelheim prison in Munich and killed in the yard by Freikorps soldiers, beaten first, then shot. Eighteen years earlier a young man with no profession met him at a utopian colony on the western edge of Berlin. Mühsam is in a cell a hundred and fifty miles away and can do nothing at all: not attend, not speak, not publish a word in his honour, not comfort the widow. He writes it in the diary instead.
stops.quote: It is so terrible! So gruesome! My friend and guide, my teacher and comrade! And here I sit, incarcerated by the same criminals who have caused his death, and I cannot help, cannot comfort anyone, cannot go to his funeral, cannot say a word in his honor.
stops.quote_source: Erich Mühsam, diary entry 'Gustav Landauer's Death', Ebrach Prison, May 1919, in Liberating Society from the State and Other Writings, ed. and trans. Gabriel Kuhn (PM Press, 2011), printed p. 128
suggested_refs: Rudolf Rocker, 'Das Ende Gustav Landauers', in Erich Mühsam et al., Gustav Landauer: Worte der Würdigung (Darmstadt: Die freie Gesellschaft), 38-39, carrying an unnamed eyewitness's report of Landauer's last words, 'Finish me off-to be human!'
sources: Liberating Society from the State and Other Writings, ed. Gabriel Kuhn (PM Press, 2011), p. 128 and footnote 4

stops.name: Ebrach, the letter from Zenzl
stops.date_confidence: attested; the diary entry headed 'Zenzl' is dated 16 May 1919 at Ebrach in the Kuhn edition, with a further entry of 19 May quoting her own letter.
stops.campa: Two weeks after the news about Landauer he learns that Zenzl is alive and at liberty. The police and the military have been through the Munich flat and taken everything in it: manuscripts, books, correspondence, the furniture of a decade. He records the loss and dismisses it in the same breath, because the only item on the inventory that mattered has been accounted for. Three days later he copies into the diary a line from her own letter, and it is the plainest sentence in the whole prison record. It would be silly to write that I love you. You know that.
stops.quote: Zenzl is alive, free, and healthy! I could not care less what the police and the military do with my things! So, they took everything. Whatever.
stops.quote_source: Erich Mühsam, diary entry 'Zenzl', Ebrach Prison, 16 May 1919, in Liberating Society from the State and Other Writings, ed. and trans. Gabriel Kuhn (PM Press, 2011), printed p. 129
suggested_refs: Zenzl Mühsam's letter of May 1919, transcribed in the Ebrach diary, Kuhn ed., printed p. 130
sources: Liberating Society from the State and Other Writings, ed. Gabriel Kuhn (PM Press, 2011), pp. 129-130

stops.name: Munich, the final statement to the court
stops.date_confidence: attested. The final statement is delivered on 11 July 1919 at the high-treason trial and first printed on 12 July 1919 in the Münchner neueste Nachrichten. The sentence, fifteen years' Festungshaft, is dated 12 July 1919 in Souchy's chronology and in Spartacus Educational. The courtroom is not named in sources consulted.
stops.campa: Brought back to Munich for a court-martial on the charge of high treason, he refuses the whole grammar of the proceeding. He does not plead mitigation. He does not ask for kindness. He tells the officers that judgment is theirs, that he has no reason to plead and only reasons to demand, and that what he demands is acquittal because nothing else makes sense. Then he tells them how long they can keep him, which is not for them to decide either. They give him fifteen years in a fortress.
stops.quote: I am the opposite of a putschist; I am a revolutionary, which means that I do not believe in coups, but in revolutions.
stops.quote_source: Erich Mühsam, Final Court Statement, Munich, 11 July 1919, in Liberating Society from the State and Other Writings, ed. and trans. Gabriel Kuhn (PM Press, 2011), printed p. 132
suggested_refs: The full Final Court Statement, Kuhn ed., pp. 131-133, including 'Revolutions cannot be stopped at random' and 'How long I will be in prison will not be determined by you'
Münchner neueste Nachrichten, 12 July 1919
sources: Liberating Society from the State and Other Writings, ed. Gabriel Kuhn (PM Press, 2011), pp. 131-133
theanarchistlibrary.org, Souchy chronology of Erich Mühsam

stops.name: Ebrach, the arithmetic of a sentence
stops.date_confidence: attested; the diary entry headed 'Sentenced' is dated 12 July 1919 at Ebrach in the Kuhn edition.
stops.campa: Back in the cell the day after the verdict he does the sum out loud in the diary and gets it comprehensively wrong. Fifteen weeks, he guesses, maybe fifteen months, because a revolution is obviously not finished and no government of this kind lasts. He serves five and a half years. The Weimar Republic he expects to be swept away outlives him, and the thing that comes after it kills him. He writes the entry at Ebrach on the twelfth of July 1919 and heads it Sentenced.
stops.quote: So now we know. If the drumhead court-martial gets its way, I will spend the next fifteen years of my life confined in a fortress. I assume that the duration will be more like fifteen weeks, maybe fifteen months.
stops.quote_source: Erich Mühsam, diary entry 'Sentenced', Ebrach Prison, 12 July 1919, in Liberating Society from the State and Other Writings, ed. and trans. Gabriel Kuhn (PM Press, 2011), printed p. 134
suggested_refs: The Ebrach prison diaries of 1919, Kuhn ed., pp. 128-141
sources: Liberating Society from the State and Other Writings, ed. Gabriel Kuhn (PM Press, 2011), p. 134

stops.name: Ansbach, the letter to Martin Andersen Nexø
stops.date_confidence: attested. The place is corrected here: the source pool gave Ebrach, which held him from April to July 1919 only; Kuhn's edition has Mühsam writing in September 1919 of 'the Ansbach Fortress, where I am currently detained'. Kuhn's footnote 63 gives the primary citation, Mühsam, In meiner Posaune muss ein Sandkorn sein: Briefe 1900-1934, ed. Gerd W. Jungblut (Vaduz: Topos, 1984), 365, confirming the date exactly. The tag is upgraded from reconstruction to attested on that footnote.
stops.campa: From the fortress at Ansbach he writes to the Danish socialist novelist Martin Andersen Nexø and explains, with no evident embarrassment, that he has joined the Communist Party in order to work against it from inside. He leaves again the following month, when the party congress votes to stand candidates in elections. The whole membership lasts about six weeks. Kuhn's footnote to the letter gives its date as the twenty-seventh of October 1919 and its source as the Jungblut edition of the correspondence.
stops.quote: I recently joined the Communist Party–of course not to follow the party line, but to be able to work against it from the inside.
stops.quote_source: Erich Mühsam, letter to Martin Andersen Nexø, 27 October 1919, quoted in Gabriel Kuhn's introduction to Liberating Society from the State and Other Writings (PM Press, 2011), printed p. 9; primary text in Mühsam, In meiner Posaune muss ein Sandkorn sein: Briefe 1900-1934, ed. Jungblut (Vaduz: Topos, 1984), 365
suggested_refs: Mühsam, In meiner Posaune muss ein Sandkorn sein: Briefe 1900-1934, ed. Gerd W. Jungblut (Vaduz: Topos, 1984)
sources: Liberating Society from the State and Other Writings, ed. Gabriel Kuhn (PM Press, 2011), p. 9 and footnotes 62-63
graswurzel.net, on the Ebrach and Ansbach stages

stops.name: Niederschönenfeld, four years and the books written in them
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the transfer date of 15 October 1920 and as to his remaining there until release. The coordinate is corrected: Niederschönenfeld sits at 48.7217, 10.9328, while the figure carried in the source pool, 48.7264, 10.8944, lands in fields about three kilometres west of the village. The play Judas and the verse collection Brennende Erde: Verse eines Kämpfers are both dated 1920.
stops.campa: He is moved to the fortress at Niederschönenfeld on the Danube in October 1920 and stays four years, under a regime harsh enough to do permanent damage to his health. He writes anyway. The play Judas comes out of these walls, and so does Brennende Erde, verses of a fighter, published while its author is serving year one of fifteen. A campaign for his release runs in the German and in the international press through all four of those years, and the sentence stands.
suggested_refs: Erich Mühsam, Judas (1920)
Erich Mühsam, Brennende Erde: Verse eines Kämpfers (1920)

stops.name: Berlin, released under the amnesty
stops.date_confidence: attested, and a contradiction in the source pool resolved in the German record's favour: the sentence was suspended on probation on 19 December 1924 and he was released on 20 December, moving to Berlin. Souchy's chronology gives March 1925 and is wrong. The total confinement is five and a half years, four of them at Niederschönenfeld, not the six years several accounts state. The coordinate marks the Anhalter Bahnhof as the likely arrival station and is not independently confirmed.
stops.campa: A general amnesty suspends the remainder of the sentence and on the twentieth of December he walks out of Niederschönenfeld and takes a train to Berlin, where a crowd is waiting at the station to meet him. He is forty-six. He has been inside for five and a half years, has lost his teacher, his journal, his city and his health, and has arrived in the capital he left as a failed pharmacist in 1900. Almost every account of the reception describes it as enormous.
suggested_refs: Press coverage of Mühsam's Berlin reception, December 1924

stops.name: Berlin, the year of two failures
stops.date_confidence: attested that Kain was restarted in 1925 and failed after a few issues, and that he was expelled from the Föderation Kommunistischer Anarchisten Deutschlands in the same year over accusations of collaborating with the KPD. No venue is specified for the expulsion and the coordinate marks central Berlin. Month and day set to order the segment.
stops.campa: He tries to restart Kain in Berlin and it dies after a handful of issues; the readership of 1913 Munich is not in the capital of 1925 and does not reassemble. In the same year the Federation of Communist Anarchists expels him for collaborating with the Communist Party. He has been out of prison for a matter of months. The republic has him under observation. The communists want him for his name, and his own federation has decided he is compromised. He goes on writing.
suggested_refs: Kain, Berlin series, 1925
Records of the Föderation Kommunistischer Anarchisten Deutschlands

stops.name: Berlin, Fanal
stops.date_confidence: attested to October 1926 in Souchy's chronology; the journal runs to 1931 and is banned by the Berlin police for four months in that final year, which is why the ban is folded into this stop rather than given one of its own. The precise editorial address is not confirmed and the coordinate marks central Berlin. The quote carried here is a reconstruction: it was seen in a secondary web summary drawing on the Kuhn volume and was not confirmed directly against the primary Fanal page.
stops.campa: In October 1926 he founds Fanal, the torch, and it becomes the most sustained anarchist attack on the Nazi movement published in Germany while publishing one is still possible. He writes it for five years. The same year he brings out Gerechtigkeit für Max Hölz, a pamphlet for an imprisoned revolutionary the whole left has found it convenient to forget, which is his standing habit: whoever is being destroyed lawfully gets the next issue. In 1931 the Berlin police, acting for a republican government under a republican press law, ban the paper for four months. The run does not recover.
stops.quote: Agitational art is good and necessary... the only art that can enthuse and enflame the proletariat is the one that derives its richness and its fire from the spirit of freedom.
stops.quote_source: Erich Mühsam, Fanal, May 1930, cited in commentary drawn from Liberating Society from the State and Other Writings, ed. Gabriel Kuhn (PM Press, 2011); not confirmed against the primary page
suggested_refs: Fanal, Berlin, 1926-1931
Erich Mühsam, Gerechtigkeit für Max Hölz (1926)
sources: theanarchistlibrary.org, Souchy chronology of Erich Mühsam
German Resistance Memorial Center (GDW Berlin), Mühsam biography

stops.name: Berlin, Piscator stages Staatsräson
stops.date_confidence: attested that Erwin Piscator directed a production of Mühsam's Staatsräson, on the execution of Sacco and Vanzetti, in Berlin in 1928. The theatre is not named in sources consulted and the coordinate marks central Berlin. Month and day set to order the segment.
stops.campa: Erwin Piscator, the loudest political director in Europe, stages Staatsräson, Mühsam's play about the electrocution of Sacco and Vanzetti in Massachusetts the previous August. A German anarchist who spent five years in a Bavarian fortress writes about two Italian anarchists killed by an American court, and Berlin comes to watch it in a house Piscator has fitted with film screens and moving stages. It is the largest audience his work reaches in his lifetime. Sacco and Vanzetti have been dead less than a year.
suggested_refs: Erich Mühsam, Staatsräson: Ein Denkmal für Sacco und Vanzetti (1928)
Erwin Piscator's Berlin productions of 1928

stops.name: Berlin-Britz, the house on the Dörchläuchtingstraße
stops.date_confidence: attested that Dörchläuchtingstraße 48 in the Hufeisensiedlung at Berlin-Britz was his residence, from the memorial stone unveiled there on 13 September 1947; the year he moved in is not established in sources consulted and the date here orders the segment only. Note an unresolved conflict: the geography lens placed his 1933 arrest at a generic central-Berlin coordinate, which cannot be reconciled with this address. Von Eisner bis Leviné is dated 1929 and Alle Wetter 1930.
stops.campa: He lives at Dörchläuchtingstraße 48 in the Hufeisensiedlung, Bruno Taut's new workers' estate at Britz on the southern edge of Berlin: modern social housing, a horseshoe of flats around a pond, built for exactly the people he writes for. Here he publishes Von Eisner bis Leviné, his own account of the Bavarian Council Republic, and writes his last play, Alle Wetter, a warning about the Nazi movement, in 1930. A memorial stone goes up on the front of the house in September 1947.
suggested_refs: Erich Mühsam, Von Eisner bis Leviné (1929)
Erich Mühsam, Alle Wetter (1930)
The memorial stone at Dörchläuchtingstraße 48, unveiled 13 September 1947

stops.name: Berlin, liberating society from the state
stops.date_confidence: attested in Souchy's chronology that Die Befreiung der Gesellschaft vom Staat was published in 1933, shortly before his final arrest; month and day are set only to order the segment, and the coordinate marks central Berlin.
stops.campa: In the last weeks in which a German anarchist can publish an argument in Germany, he publishes Die Befreiung der Gesellschaft vom Staat, the clearest statement he ever makes of the single position he has held since he was seventeen: that the state is the machine that produces the injustice of every other institution, and that nothing whatever is fixed until it is dismantled. The pamphlet appears. Hitler is appointed Chancellor on the thirtieth of January.
suggested_refs: Erich Mühsam, Die Befreiung der Gesellschaft vom Staat: Was ist kommunistischer Anarchismus? (1933)
sources: theanarchistlibrary.org, Souchy chronology of Erich Mühsam
Liberating Society from the State and Other Writings, ed. Gabriel Kuhn (PM Press, 2011)

stops.name: Berlin-Britz, the arrest after the Reichstag fire
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the arrest, in the early hours of 28 February 1933 by the SA, hours after the Reichstag fire of 27 February, in the mass roundup of political opponents. The address is not settled: this stop uses the Dörchläuchtingstraße 48 residence pin, while the geography lens gave a generic central-Berlin figure of 52.51, 13.39 for the same event. One of the two is wrong and the contradiction is left open. Joseph Goebbels singles him out publicly as a Jewish subversive.
stops.campa: The Reichstag burns on the evening of the twenty-seventh. In the small hours of the twenty-eighth the SA come to the flat and take him and beat him, one name on a list drawn up long in advance. Goebbels names him publicly as a Jewish subversive, which in the vocabulary of that February is an instruction to whoever holds him. He is fifty-four years old and will not be free again. Friends had urged him for weeks to leave Germany and a train ticket to Prague is said to have been bought; he did not use it.
suggested_refs: The Reichstag Fire Decree of 28 February 1933 and the mass arrest lists prepared under it
sources: German Resistance Memorial Center (GDW Berlin), Mühsam biography

stops.name: Berlin-Moabit, the jail on the Lehrter Straße
stops.date_confidence: attested as the first stage of custody in the GDW Berlin sequence and the erichinenglish chronology; month and day set to order the segment.
stops.campa: The first stage is the ordinary Prussian remand jail on the Lehrter Straße in Moabit: a building with a governor, a register, printed rules and a legal basis, which is what distinguishes it from everywhere he is taken afterwards. Four more institutions follow in seventeen months, each standing further outside the law than the one before. He is held here without charge under the emergency decree signed on the morning of his arrest, the decree that suspends the articles of the constitution guaranteeing personal liberty.
suggested_refs: The Lehrter Straße remand prison, Berlin-Moabit
sources: German Resistance Memorial Center (GDW Berlin), Mühsam biography

stops.name: Sonnenburg, the first camp
stops.date_confidence: attested; Mühsam appears in the prisoner list of KZ Sonnenburg. The coordinate is corrected: the camp stood at Sonnenburg, today Słońsk in Poland near Kostrzyn, at 52.5644, 14.8100, and the figure carried in the source pool, 52.6167, 15.1167, lies about twenty-five kilometres away in open country. Tom Goyens, translating Rudolf Rocker's Der Leidensweg von Zensl Mühsam (1949), places Zenzl's visit and the parting words in May 1933; month set accordingly, day set to order the segment.
stops.campa: Sonnenburg is one of the improvised camps the SA opens in the first months of the regime: a disused Prussian penitentiary east of the Oder, staffed by men with no training, no supervision and a list of writers and deputies whose names they know from the newspapers. He is beaten here as a matter of routine, and singled out for it, because his name is on the list twice, once as an anarchist and once as a Jew. Zenzl is permitted a visit in May. At the end of it, with guards standing over them both, he gives her the one sentence he wants her to keep.
stops.quote: Remember this, Zensl: I will certainly never be a coward.
stops.quote_source: Erich Mühsam to Zenzl Mühsam at Sonnenburg, May 1933, in Rudolf Rocker, Der Leidensweg von Zensl Mühsam (Berlin: Verlag Die Freie Gesellschaft, 1949), trans. Tom Goyens, 'I Will Never Be a Coward: The Last Months of Erich Mühsam', Anarchistories
suggested_refs: The prisoner list of KZ Sonnenburg, 1933
Rudolf Rocker, Der Leidensweg von Zensl Mühsam (1949)
sources: tomgoyens.substack.com, 'I Will Never Be a Coward: The Last Months of Erich Mühsam'

stops.name: Berlin-Plötzensee, back inside the prison system
stops.date_confidence: attested as a stage in the GDW Berlin sequence, between Sonnenburg and Brandenburg. The coordinate is corrected: Plötzensee prison stands on the Friedrich-Olbricht-Damm in Charlottenburg-Nord at 52.5403, 13.3216, and the figure in the source pool, 52.5386, 13.2953, falls about 1.8 kilometres west in the Westhafen area. Month and day set to order the segment.
stops.campa: He is moved back into Berlin, to Plötzensee, and the shuttling between camp and prison is itself part of the method: no charge, no term, no hearing, no address that a lawyer or a wife can rely on for more than a few weeks at a time. Zenzl spends 1933 finding out where her husband is and travelling there. Plötzensee will become, later in the regime, the execution house of the German resistance. In the autumn of 1933 it is only a stopping place, and he is transferred out of it again before the year ends.
suggested_refs: Justizvollzugsanstalt Plötzensee, Friedrich-Olbricht-Damm, Berlin
sources: German Resistance Memorial Center (GDW Berlin), Mühsam biography

stops.name: Brandenburg an der Havel, the slow murdering
stops.date_confidence: attested; Mühsam is named in the prisoner list of KZ Brandenburg, which occupied the old penitentiary at Neuendorfer Straße 90, today Nicolaiplatz 28/30, at 52.4107, 12.5506. The source pool's 52.4125, 12.5316 lies about 1.3 kilometres west. A contradiction is left open here: the GDW Berlin sequence has him reaching Oranienburg in early October 1933, while Goyens, following Rocker, places this whispered exchange at Brandenburg in October or November 1933 and the transfer to Oranienburg in February 1934. Both cannot be right.
stops.campa: The camp at Brandenburg an der Havel is the old penitentiary on the Neuendorfer Straße, taken over by the SA in 1933, and the beatings there are routine and administered on a schedule. Zenzl is allowed in on restricted visits, watched, timed, forbidden to touch him. During one of them, after she has heard what is done to him daily, he tells her in a whisper what he is afraid of and what he is not. The exchange reaches us only through her own testimony, given to Rudolf Rocker after the war and printed by him in 1949.
stops.quote: You know, Zensl, I am not afraid of dying, but this slow murdering, that is what is dreadful.
stops.quote_source: Erich Mühsam to Zenzl Mühsam at Brandenburg, October or November 1933, in Rudolf Rocker, Der Leidensweg von Zensl Mühsam (Berlin: Verlag Die Freie Gesellschaft, 1949), trans. Tom Goyens, 'I Will Never Be a Coward: The Last Months of Erich Mühsam', Anarchistories
suggested_refs: The prisoner list of KZ Brandenburg, 1933-1934
sources: tomgoyens.substack.com, 'I Will Never Be a Coward: The Last Months of Erich Mühsam'

stops.name: Oranienburg, prisoner number 2651
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the photograph: USHMM holds the identification photograph taken at Oranienburg on 3 February 1934, prisoner number 2651. The arrival date is contradictory and the contradiction is left open: GDW Berlin has him reaching Oranienburg in early October 1933, four months before the photograph, while Goyens, following Rocker, has the transfer in February 1934. The coordinate is corrected to the camp itself, the former brewery on the Berliner Straße at 52.7493, 13.2370; the source pool's 52.7547, 13.2364 sits in the town centre north of the camp.
stops.campa: KZ Oranienburg is a disused brewery on the Berliner Straße run by the SA, and the registration photograph taken there on the third of February 1934 shows a man of fifty-five whose right eye has been destroyed and whose face has been broken. He is prisoner 2651. The photograph is an administrative document, taken because the camp needs a record of the man it holds, and it is the clearest surviving evidence of what the camp has already done to him. The commanders send for him repeatedly through the spring and summer. A fellow inmate, John Stone, records what he says on coming back from one of those interviews.
stops.quote: They want me to hang myself-but I will not do them the favor.
stops.quote_source: Erich Mühsam at Oranienburg, reported by the inmate John Stone, in Liberating Society from the State and Other Writings, ed. and trans. Gabriel Kuhn (PM Press, 2011), printed p. 16
suggested_refs: USHMM photo archive, 'Erich Muehsam', identification photograph, Oranienburg, 3 February 1934
sources: German Resistance Memorial Center (GDW Berlin), Mühsam biography
Liberating Society from the State and Other Writings, ed. Gabriel Kuhn (PM Press, 2011), p. 16

stops.name: Oranienburg, the last visit
stops.date_confidence: attested as to date and place. Zenzl travelled to Oranienburg with about a hundred and fifty women against a visitation ban and won each prisoner a supervised ten-minute visit. The wording is carried as it can be verified: Goyens's text reads 'whatever may happen, never believe that I committed suicide', without the vocative 'Zensl' that some retellings prepend. The whole exchange reaches us through Zenzl's testimony as relayed by Rocker.
stops.campa: On the eighth of July Zenzl arrives at the camp gate with about a hundred and fifty other women, in defiance of a ban on visits, and the SA give way far enough to allow each prisoner ten supervised minutes. She gets her ten minutes and he spends them on two instructions. The first is to make the foreign countries mobilise, because every man inside is in danger. The second is about what she is to refuse to believe, whatever she is told and by whom. He has been asked to hang himself and has said no, and he has two days left.
stops.quote: whatever may happen, never believe that I committed suicide.
stops.quote_source: Erich Mühsam to Zenzl Mühsam at Oranienburg, 8 July 1934, in Rudolf Rocker, Der Leidensweg von Zensl Mühsam (Berlin: Verlag Die Freie Gesellschaft, 1949), trans. Tom Goyens, 'I Will Never Be a Coward: The Last Months of Erich Mühsam', Anarchistories
suggested_refs: Rudolf Rocker, Der Leidensweg von Zensl Mühsam (Berlin: Verlag Die Freie Gesellschaft, 1949)
sources: tomgoyens.substack.com, 'I Will Never Be a Coward: The Last Months of Erich Mühsam'

stops.name: Oranienburg, the latrine
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the killing; the date is contradictory and the contradiction is not resolved. English Wikipedia gives the night of 9-10 July 1934, Spartacus Educational and Encyclopedia.com give 10 July, USHMM gives 11 July. The majority and the German record give the night of 9-10 July, and 10 July is used here to order the file. The camp administration ruled it suicide; prisoner eyewitnesses reported that he had been beaten and strangled and the hanging staged afterwards. KZ Oranienburg was dissolved four days later, on 14 July 1934.
stops.campa: In the night of the ninth to the tenth of July an SS detachment takes him from his block. His body is found hanging in a latrine and the camp administration enters suicide in the record. Prisoners who see him say he had been beaten and strangled first and the rope arranged afterwards. He had told his wife two days earlier exactly what would be claimed and exactly what she was to do about it. He is fifty-six. The camp is dissolved four days later, on the fourteenth of July.
suggested_refs: Prisoner testimony on the killing of Erich Mühsam, collected in the Sachsenhausen memorial's documentation of the 1933-1934 Oranienburg camp
sources: German Resistance Memorial Center (GDW Berlin), Mühsam biography

stops.name: Berlin-Dahlem, the Waldfriedhof
stops.date_confidence: attested as to burial at the Waldfriedhof Dahlem on 16 July 1934, grave Feld 015-479, Abteilung 2A, Nr. 144. Two corrections are folded in: the afterlife lens gave the grave field as 006-21-15, which is wrong, and gave the coordinate as 52.4547, 13.2764, which conflicts with the geography lens's 52.4544, 13.2632 for the same cemetery; the latter is used and the discrepancy is recorded here rather than resolved.
stops.campa: He is buried at the Waldfriedhof in Dahlem on the sixteenth of July, in Feld 015-479. Zenzl is barred from the funeral. The same day she crosses into Czechoslovakia with help from the journalist Dorothy Thompson, carrying his diaries and manuscripts, and in August 1935 she carries them on to Moscow, where a Soviet publishing cooperative has promised an edition. The papers go into an archive instead. Several volumes, among them 1910-11 and 1916-19, are never seen again.
suggested_refs: The critical edition of Mühsam's diaries, Verbrecher Verlag, Berlin, 15 volumes, 2011-2019, and the editorial notes at muehsam-tagebuch.de on the volumes lost in the USSR
sources: German Resistance Memorial Center (GDW Berlin), Mühsam biography

stops.name: Lübeck, the stone in the pavement
stops.date_confidence: attested. The Erich-Mühsam-Gesellschaft was founded at Lübeck on 6 April 1989, the hundred and eleventh anniversary of his birth. The Stolperstein in the old town, in front of the Buddenbrookhaus, was laid in 2003. The stop is placed at his childhood city, where he actually lived; the later commemorations are cited as engagement with that place, not staged as scenes of their own.
stops.campa: The city that expelled him from its Gymnasium in 1896 founds a society in his name on the hundred and eleventh anniversary of his birth, and sets a brass Stolperstein into the pavement of the old town in 2003, a few steps from the Buddenbrook house. Zenzl outlives him by twenty-eight years: arrested in Moscow in 1936 as a Trotskyist, eight years' hard labour at Potma, exile, re-imprisonment, release in 1954, East Berlin, death in 1962. Her remains join his in the Dahlem grave in the autumn of 1992.
suggested_refs: The Erich-Mühsam-Gesellschaft, Lübeck, erich-muehsam.de
The Stolperstein for Erich Mühsam, Lübeck old town, 2003
Slime, Sich fügen heißt lügen (2012), setting Mühsam's poems to music
